title: Even some Reformed who signed Dort admit it: Gomarus on Tyre's repentance (Matthew 11:21), cited by Walaeus
source_text: XXV. Sed & inter Reformatos qui Dordracenae Synodo subscribunt, reperiuntur nonnulli agnoscentes in Deo scientiam illam conditionatam, per quam ante omne voluntatis suae decretum, novit quid causa libera quaelibet, in quovis rerum ordine, pro ingenita sibi libertate, factura esset. Inter quos primum numerandus videtur Franciscus ille Gomarus, in hanc sententiam jam a Curcellaeo citatus. Etenim scribens in locum Matth. 11. v. 21. Postquam observavit Tyriorum Poenitentiam, posita miraculorum Christi conditione, futuram, intelligi hujusmodi, quae communis est Electis & Reprobis, credentibus & non credentibus: qualis, ex ejus mente, fuit Ninivitarum cum sacco Poenitentia; subjungit haec ipsa verba, Quod autem Christus de futura hac Tyriorum, posita illa conditione, poenitentia asserit, illius veritas ex indefinita divinae ipsius naturae praescientia constat, qua novit quidnam, quo posito antecedente, fuisset secuturum, etiamsi neutrum evenerit. Nam posita ea conditione, alterutrum fuisse eventurum, ut aut poenitentiam agerent, aut non agerent, omnibus notum est ex principio illo, quod duo opposita non possunt esse simul vera: sed utrum eorum fuisset futurum, cum res fuerit contingens, solus praevidit, qui infinita sua scientia omnia videt, nec solum necessaria, sed etiam futura contingentia certo praedicit. Similis locus est Ezech. 3. v. 6, 7. Ut refert Baldvinus Walaeus commentario suo in libros historicos Novi Testamenti ad locum Matthaei citatum.
pass_a_gloss: XXV. But also among the Reformed who subscribe to the Synod of Dort, some are found acknowledging in God that conditional knowledge, by which before every decree of his will, he knows what any free cause, in any order of things, according to the liberty inborn in it, would do. Among whom first that Franciscus Gomarus seems to be numbered, already cited by Curcellaeus for this opinion. For writing on the place Matt. 11, v. 21. After he observed that the Penitence of the Tyrians, the condition of Christ's miracles being posited, future, is understood to be of this kind, which is common to the Elect and Reprobate, to believers and unbelievers: such, in his mind, was the Penitence of the Ninevites with sackcloth; he subjoins these very words, But what Christ asserts of this future penitence of the Tyrians, that condition being posited, its truth stands firm from the indefinite foreknowledge of his divine nature, by which he knows what, an antecedent being posited, would have followed, even if neither came to pass. For that condition being posited, that one or the other would have come to pass, that they either would do penitence, or would not, is known to all from that principle, that two opposites cannot be true at once: but which of them would have been future, since the thing was contingent, he alone foresaw, who sees all things by his infinite knowledge, and certainly foretells not only necessary things, but also future contingents. A similar place is Ezek. 3, v. 6, 7. As Baldvinus Walaeus reports in his commentary on the historical books of the New Testament at the place of Matthew cited.
pass_b_english: Even among the Reformed who subscribe to the Synod of Dort, some acknowledge in God this conditional knowledge, by which, before every decree of his will, he knows what any free cause would do in any order of things, according to its innate freedom. Francis Gomarus seems to come first among them, and Courcelles has already cited him for this view.

Commenting on Matthew 11:21, Gomarus first notes that the repentance of Tyre that would have followed Christ's miracles is to be understood as the kind common to elect and reprobate, believers and unbelievers. In his view the sackcloth repentance of the Ninevites was of this kind. He then adds these very words:

'What Christ asserts about this repentance of Tyre that would have followed under that condition is true by virtue of the unbounded foreknowledge of his divine nature. By it he knows what would have followed given an antecedent, even if neither came about. Given that condition, everyone knows that one or the other would have happened, that they would either repent or not, from the principle that two opposites cannot both be true at once. But which of them would have happened, since the matter was contingent, only he foresaw who sees all things by his infinite knowledge and foretells with certainty not only necessary things but future contingents too. A similar passage is Ezekiel 3:6-7.'
So Balduinus Walaeus reports in his commentary on the historical books of the New Testament, at the passage of Matthew cited.
